articles.intro: 200-240 word intro distinguishing no-show fee policy from cancellation policy. Cancellation policies cover when clients tell you they cannot make it. sections.title: What makes a no-show fee enforceable

sections.directives: Provide template language inside callout block. 4-6 sentences: 'If you do not arrive within [X] minutes of your appointment time without notice, the full cost of the service will be charged to the card on file. sections.directives: Exact script. 'Hi [name], we missed you at your [X:XX] appointment today. As per the booking policy, the $[X] no-show fee will be charged to the card on file. Reply if you'd like to rebook with a fresh slot.' Factual, warm, brief. How to handle response. 200-240 words.

sections.title: Winning Stripe disputes on no-show charges
sections.directives: Practical playbook. When dispute comes in: (1) Stripe gives 7 days to respond, (2) upload screenshots of policy at booking, confirmation email, reminder, booking timeline, (3) Stripe rules within 60-75 days. Most clean documentation wins. Cite that 75-85% of well-documented disputes resolved in your favor. 220-260 words.

sections.title: Handling repeat offenders without burning the relationship
sections.directives: Three-strike system: (1) first no-show, charge and offer rebook, (2) second no-show, charge plus require deposit on all future bookings, (3) third no-show, decline future bookings or require full prepayment. SMS language for 'we need to require deposits going forward' conversation. Warm but firm. 220-260 words.

faqs.q: Can a client refuse to pay a no-show fee?
faqs.answerHint: They can dispute charge with bank, but if documentation is clean, dispute usually resolves in your favor. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: Should the no-show fee be 100% of the service?
faqs.answerHint: Yes. Chair was empty, loss was total. Lesser amounts signal policy is negotiable. 30-50 words.

faqs.q: What if the client never gave a card at booking?

faqs.q: What is the grace period before someone counts as a no-show?
faqs.answerHint: Standard is 15 minutes for short services, 20-30 minutes for long ones. State explicitly in policy. 30-50 words.

faqs.q: Can I waive a no-show fee?
faqs.answerHint: Yes, for genuine emergencies with brief context. Don't waive for 'something came up' or vague reasons. Inconsistent waiving breaks the policy. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: What if a client says they texted to cancel?
faqs.answerHint: Texts to a personal number don't count if policy requires cancellation through booking system. State that explicitly in policy. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: Are no-show fees taxable income?
faqs.answerHint: Yes in most jurisdictions. Treat as service revenue in bookkeeping. Talk to accountant for state-specific rules. 30-50 words.

Real booking platform with: (1) availability shown live, (2) deposits collected upfront, (3) automated confirmations and reminders, (4) cancellation policy disclosed at booking, (5) client list owned by you. Single change adds 4-6 hours per week back to owner. Link /platform/tools/notifications/ and /platform/tools/payments/. 220-260 words.

sections.title: Pricing the salon (and raising prices without losing clients)
sections.directives: Strategic advice on pricing. (1) audit current pricing against local market every 12 months, (2) raise prices in 8-12% increments not 20% jumps, (3) raise on new clients first, give existing clients 60 days notice, (4) tier services by skill level (junior, senior, master). Reference that most salons underprice by 15-30%. 240-280 words.

sections.title: Retention math: keep more clients before chasing new ones
sections.directives: Hard truth. Acquiring new salon client costs $30-80 in marketing. Keeping existing one costs roughly $0. Yet most salons spend on acquisition and lose 30% of clients every 12 months. Three retention levers: (1) rebook at checkout (industry best practice), (2) automated 4-week re-engagement, (3) personal text from stylist at 8 weeks if no rebook. Link /features/growth/winback/. 240-280 words.

sections.title: When to hire your first stylist (and how to structure it)
sections.directives: Practical milestones. Hire when: (1) turning away clients 2+ times per week, (2) working over 50 hours/week consistently, (3) have 8-12 weeks of booked-out runway. Three structures: (1) booth rental (lowest risk, lowest control), (2) commission (medium risk, medium control), (3) hourly + commission (highest control, highest overhead). BookReady opinion: start with booth rental, transition to commission when you can afford to. 280-320 words.

sections.title: When brand actually starts driving growth
sections.directives: Honest take. Brand starts mattering past 2-3 stylists. Before that, you are the brand. (1) designed website on your own domain is single biggest brand lever for under $300/yr, (2) consistent Instagram aesthetic compounds slowly but reliably, (3) salon's physical interior matters less than photos of it online. Link /templates/ and /platform/website/templates/. 240-280 words.

sections.title: Multi-location salon: when to consider it, when to wait
sections.directives: Reality check. Second location works when: (1) first location runs profitably without you for 90 days straight, (2) you have deputy who can manage operations, (3) you have $80,000-150,000 in capital reserves. Most second locations fail because first is not yet self-sustaining. 220-260 words.

sections.title: Marketing channels that actually work for salons (and the ones that do not)
sections.directives: Practical channels. Works: (1) Instagram organic with consistent reels (most efficient), (2) Google Business Profile with reviews, (3) referral program for existing clients, (4) local partnerships. Doesn't work for most salons: (1) Facebook ads (high CAC for service businesses), (2) influencer 'collabs' that cost more in services than they bring back, (3) Yelp ads. Link /features/growth/reviews/ and /features/growth/email/. 280-320 words.

faqs.q: How much revenue should I have before hiring my first stylist?
faqs.answerHint: Aim for $8,000-12,000/mo solo before adding a chair. Need to know demand is real and recurring, not seasonal. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: How often should I raise prices?
faqs.answerHint: Audit every 12 months, raise in 8-12% increments. Avoid 20%+ jumps which break client trust. Give 60 days notice to existing clients. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: Is booth rental or commission better?
faqs.answerHint: Booth rental is lower risk and easier to start. Commission gives you more control of brand and standards. Most salons start with booth and grow into commission. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: What is a healthy retention rate for a hair salon?
faqs.answerHint: 70-80% annual client retention is solid. Above 85% is exceptional and usually means you have system right. Below 60% means there is a leak. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: How long until a second location is profitable?
faqs.answerHint: Most second locations take 8-14 months to break even. Plan for 12-month runway minimum and have capital reserves through that period. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: Should I focus on Instagram or Google for new clients?
faqs.answerHint: Both, in that order. Instagram drives discovery (especially for color and lash), Google captures local search intent. Run both, prioritize whichever your local market favors. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: How do I keep my best stylists from leaving?
faqs.answerHint: Pay above market, give them visibility on website, build their personal brand, run the salon like a place they would recommend to a friend. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: What is the single biggest growth lever for a 1-chair salon?
faqs.answerHint: Retention systems. Auto-rebook at checkout plus 4-week reminder is worth more than any Instagram campaign for small salons. 30-50 words.
